--- title: "What's new for time-to-event data in tidymodels" subtitle: "uRos 2026, Paris" author: "Hannah Frick, Posit" format: revealjs: slide-number: true show-slide-number: all footer: theme: [default, style.scss] css: styles.css highlight-style: a11y width: 1280 height: 720 knitr: opts_chunk: echo: true collapse: true comment: "#>" fig.align: center --- ## Budget participatif :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - Every year since 2014, Parisians propose and vote on projects - Greening a schoolyard, a new playground, a sports facility, ... - **How long from the vote until the project opens?** ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](images/hopscotch-eric-tompkins-unsplash.jpg){height="540" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Colourful numbered stepping stones of a hopscotch game in a playground"} ::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.5em"} Photo by [Eric Tompkins](https://unsplash.com/@erictompkins) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/multicolored-number-boards-tRIw6cFSs2E) ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} - city tracks every project from studies through to opening ::: ## The data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} glimpse(projects) #> Rows: 1,375 #> Columns: 11 #> $ project "3788", "2960", "3594", "12374", "3801", "100… #> $ months 109.23333, 26.00000, 103.00000, 13.23333, 36.… #> $ opened FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, … #> $ theme "social", "sport", "safety", "cleanliness", "… #> $ department "economy", "youth and sports", "roads", "clea… #> $ scale "city-wide", "arrondissement", "arrondissemen… #> $ arrondissement "several", "01", "01", "several", "several", … #> $ priority_share 0.1264368, 0.0000000, 0.0000000, 0.0000000, 1… #> $ edition 2017, 2016, 2017, 2025, 2017, 2021, 2018, 202… #> $ budget 3500000, 200000, 155000, 120000, 3500000, 200… #> $ n_operations 87, 1, 1, 3, 21, 8, 8, 1, 11, 24, 28, 39, 229… ``` ::: [Source: Ville de Paris, opendata.paris.fr, licence ODbL]{style="font-size: 0.6em"} ::: {.notes} - one row per project, editions 2014–2025 (no 2020 edition) - a project counts as open once all of its operations (sites) are open - months: from the vote until opening, or until today if it's not open yet ::: ## Time to event ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/swimmer-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - we know it's taken *at least* this long, not how long it will take ::: ## Everything is an event? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/swimmer-all-events-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1056} ::: ::: Use the observed time as if every project had opened
→ underestimates the time until opening ::: {.notes} - plain regression on the observed time - the projects still waiting are treated as if they opened today ::: ## Drop the ones still waiting? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/swimmer-drop-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1056} ::: ::: Only use projects that have opened
→ throws away data, and biased: the slow ones are the ones still waiting ::: {.notes} - not missing at random - here: almost 40% are not open yet! - especially recent editions would be left with only their fastest projects ::: ## Survival analysis - The right tool for _censored regression_ - Despite the name, the event can be loads of things: - A project opening - A business closing - Leaving unemployment or benefits - A household responding during fieldwork ::: {.notes} ::: ## Kaplan-Meier curve ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/km-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - Time = Months since the vote - Survival prob = prob the project is not yet open - ticks: censored projects, they count as "still waiting" up until they leave the data ::: ## tidymodels ![](images/hex/rsample.png){.absolute top="200" left="0" width="150"} ![](images/hex/recipes.png){.absolute top="200" left="250" width="150"} ![](images/hex/workflows.png){.absolute top="200" left="400" width="150"} ![](images/hex/parsnip.png){.absolute top="200" left="550" width="150"} ![](images/hex/yardstick.png){.absolute top="200" left="800" width="150"} ![](images/hex/tune.png){.absolute top="200" left="1050" width="150"} ![](images/hex/tidymodels.png){.absolute top="400" left="825" width="250"} ::: {.notes} - a framework for statistical modelling and machine learning - we take care of the procedural code / boilerplate, so you can focus on the modelling question - consistent interfaces make it easy to explore options: models, preprocessing, metrics, tuning - guardrails against pitfalls such as data leakage make it safe - (click) censored: survival analysis across the whole framework ::: . . . ![](images/hex/censored.png){.absolute top="333" left="626" width="150"} ## Setting up ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-2|4-7|9-12|14-16"} projects <- projects |> mutate(opening_time = Surv(months, opened), .keep = "unused") set.seed(403) projects_split <- initial_split(projects, prop = 0.8) projects_train <- training(projects_split) projects_folds <- vfold_cv(projects_train, v = 10) projects_rec <- recipe(opening_time ~ ., data = projects_train) |> update_role(project, new_role = "id") |> step_log(budget, n_operations) |> step_other(arrondissement, theme, threshold = 0.02) cox_spec <- proportional_hazards() |> set_engine("survival") |> set_mode("censored regression") ``` ::: ::: {.notes} ::: # What's new: models ## Two new engines for random forests ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1,5|2,6|1-7"} ranger_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("censored regression") rfsrc_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("randomForestSRC") |> set_mode("censored regression") ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - switching model type or engine is one line - why these? they are fast - why random forests? generally work well out of the box - but also: why tree-based models? censored has quite a few of those! - censored smooths over engine quirks, e.g. randomForestSRC's 0/1 status coding and pre-made Surv responses in recipes ::: ## Survival trees ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/tree-illustration-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - a forest averages many such trees - each leaf holds a survival curve, not a single number - flexible: no proportional hazards assumption - data-driven groupings ::: ## A null model as your true baseline ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} null_spec <- null_model() |> set_engine("survival") |> set_mode("censored regression") ``` ::: - Ignores all predictors: one Kaplan-Meier curve for everyone - Does your model beat doing nothing? ## The same prediction for everyone {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} null_wflow <- workflow(projects_rec, null_spec) null_fit <- fit(null_wflow, data = projects_train) predict(null_fit, slice(testing(projects_split), 1:3), type = "time") #> # A tibble: 3 × 1 #> .pred_time #> #> 1 46 #> 2 46 #> 3 46 ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - three different projects, same predicted time: the median of the Kaplan-Meier curve ::: ## Predicting survival probabilities {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} null_pred <- predict( null_fit, slice(testing(projects_split), 1:3), type = "survival", eval_time = c(12, 24, 36, 48) ) null_pred$.pred[[1]] #> # A tibble: 4 × 2 #> .eval_time .pred_survival #> #> 1 12 0.92 #> 2 24 0.752 #> 3 36 0.586 #> 4 48 0.472 ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - probability of not being open yet, at chosen points in time (here every year) - one tibble per project, nested in .pred: still one row per project - the same for every project with the null model - this is the type of prediction the Brier score works with ::: ## Resampling the null model ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} null_wflow <- workflow(projects_rec, null_spec) projects_metrics <- metric_set( brier_survival, brier_survival_integrated, concordance_survival ) null_res <- fit_resamples( null_wflow, resamples = projects_folds, metrics = projects_metrics, eval_time = 1:96 ) ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - we take care of the procedural code: 10 fits, predictions on the held-out folds, metrics at 96 time points, collected for you - Brier score: how close the predicted probability is to what happened, at time t (lower is better) - every month for the first 8 years; longer than that, only the earliest editions are followed up and estimates get noisy ::: ## The baseline ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/null-brier-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - the Brier score of the null model over time - low at first: almost no project opens in the first months, easy to predict - peaks when it's hardest to tell who's still waiting ::: ## Many models at once ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} projects_res <- workflow_set( preproc = list(rec = projects_rec), models = list( null = null_spec, cox = cox_spec, ranger = ranger_spec, rfsrc = rfsrc_spec ) ) |> workflow_map( "fit_resamples", resamples = projects_folds, metrics = projects_metrics, eval_time = 1:96, seed = 1 ) ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - we take care of the procedural code, again: 4 models × 10 folds - you focus on the modelling choices: preprocessing, models, metrics - link to production: a short declarative specification instead of hand-written loops - easier to review, easy to rerun when next year's data arrives - auditable, reproducible, same code gives same results ::: ## Every model beats the baseline ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/brier-over-time-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - ranger: The cause is ranger's default minimum node size of 3 for survival forests. Tiny terminal nodes keep survival curves flat at high values in the tail. ::: ## The final model {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} best_id <- rank_results( projects_res, rank_metric = "brier_survival_integrated" ) |> slice_head(n = 1) |> pull(wflow_id) final_fit <- projects_res |> extract_workflow(best_id) |> last_fit(projects_split, metrics = projects_metrics, eval_time = 1:96) ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - OPTIONAL slide - rank by integrated Brier score, take the best workflow - last_fit(): fit on all of the training data, evaluate once on the test data ::: ## Predictions are survival curves {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/example-curves-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - OPTIONAL slide - one curve per project, from the best model - all from the same edition, so the differences come from theme and budget ::: # Built to be extended ## We extend ![](images/hex/rsample.png){.absolute top="200" left="0" width="150"} ![](images/hex/recipes.png){.absolute top="200" left="250" width="150"} ![](images/hex/workflows.png){.absolute top="200" left="400" width="150"} ![](images/hex/parsnip.png){.absolute top="200" left="550" width="150"} ![](images/hex/yardstick.png){.absolute top="200" left="800" width="150"} ![](images/hex/tune.png){.absolute top="200" left="1050" width="150"} . . . ![](images/hex/spatialsample.png){.absolute top="333" left="76" width="150"} ![](images/hex/textrecipes.png){.absolute top="333" left="326" width="150"} ![](images/hex/embed.png){.absolute top="466" left="250" width="150"} ![](images/hex/workflowsets.png){.absolute top="333" left="476" width="150"} ![](images/hex/censored.png){.absolute top="333" left="626" width="150"} ![](images/hex/finetune.png){.absolute top="333" left="1126" width="150"} ::: {.notes} - tidymodels is built to be extended - we have extended the core packages ourselves: spatialsample, recipes extensions, parsnip extensions, workflowsets, finetune - not much for yardstick so far ::: ## You extend: developer articles [![](images/tidymodels-learn-developer-tools.png){height="500" fig-align="center"}](https://www.tidymodels.org/learn/#category=developer%20tools) []{style="font-size: 0.6em"} ::: {.notes} - you can build your own: models, engines, recipe steps, metrics, tidiers - we've written down how: tidymodels.org, Learn, developer tools ::: ## You extend: checklists [![](images/parsnip-dev-checklists.png){height="500" fig-align="center"}](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/articles/checklists.html) []{style="font-size: 0.6em"} ::: {.notes} - the checklists we use ourselves, for new models and engines - in the Articles menu of the parsnip website - recipes has one for new steps: ::: ## You extend: skills [![](images/tidymodels-skills.png){height="500" fig-align="center"}](https://skills.tidymodels.org) []{style="font-size: 0.6em"} ::: {.notes} - Claude Code skills for tidymodels: for using it, and for creating extensions following our practices ::: ## Something missing? Ask us! [![](images/issue-551.png){width="820" fig-align="center"}](https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/issues/551) . . . → yardstick: a new metric type for the linear predictor, and `royston_survival()` ::: {.notes} - a user wanted to write their own metrics on the linear predictor - that wasn't possible: no metric type triggered that kind of prediction - they asked, we built it - they also wanted Royston and Sauerbrei's metric, so we added that as well - the same user also asked for easier access to censoring weights in predict() (parsnip #1371) ::: ## Royston's metric {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} workflow(projects_rec, cox_spec) |> fit_resamples( projects_folds, metrics = metric_set(royston_survival, concordance_survival) ) |> collect_metrics() #> # A tibble: 2 × 6 #> .metric .estimator mean n std_err .config #> #> 1 concordance_survival standard 0.736 10 0.0107 pre0_mod0_post0 #> 2 royston_survival standard 0.355 10 0.0205 pre0_mod0_post0 ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - how well the linear predictor separates the projects - mixes with existing metric types in the same metric set - needs a linear predictor: Cox, Weibull, boosted tree, but not the forests or the null model - royston_survival() reports R²_D, the explained-variation version of D ::: ## What's new - Random forests via `"ranger"` and `"randomForestSRC"` - A null model as a baseline - A new metric type for the linear predictor, and Royston-Sauerbrei's metric - Also new: faster tuning for boosted trees, censoring weights in `predict()`
::: {.notes} - boosted trees with mboost: multi_predict(), so tune_grid() fits one model per number of trees ::: ## Durations with unfinished cases? - Censored regression in tidymodels works just like classification or regression - If something is missing, you can extend the framework, or ask us
::: {style="text-align: center"} ::: # Backup {visibility="uncounted"} ## Case weights {visibility="uncounted"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |model |with case weights |without | |:----------------------|:----------------------------------------|:-------| |proportional_hazards() |survival, glmnet | | |survival_reg() |survival, flexsurv, flexsurvspline | | |decision_tree() |rpart, partykit | | |bag_tree() | |rpart | |boost_tree() | |mboost | |rand_forest() |partykit, aorsf, ranger, randomForestSRC | | ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - censored 0.4.0: bag_tree() with rpart and boost_tree() with mboost no longer accept case weights - ipred errors with weights; mboost fits with weights but can't predict from those fits ::: ## Coming from SAS {visibility="uncounted"} | SAS | R/tidymodels | |---|---| | `PROC LIFETEST` | `survival::survfit()`, `null_model()` | | `PROC PHREG` | `proportional_hazards()` | | `PROC LIFEREG` | `survival_reg()` | ::: {.notes} - same models, different defaults: PHREG uses Breslow for ties (R: Efron), LIFETEST uses log-log CIs (R: log) ::: ## Data caveats {visibility="uncounted"} - Opening dates are given to the month - The vote is approximated as 1 October of the edition year - Source: Ville de Paris, *Budget participatif : opérations des projets gagnants et réalisations*, opendata.paris.fr, licence ODbL ## Abandoned projects {visibility="uncounted"} - About 5% of operations are abandoned: they will never open - That's a competing risk; here we dropped them

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
